He also lied about a few of the weapons saying they had been destroyed but were later found by agents. On 3 April 2003, a federal grand jury returned a second superseding indictment which charged Shannahan with eleven counts of unlawfully transferring a firearm, in violation of 26:5861(e), and one count of making a false statement, in violation of 18:1001(a)(2). On August 13th, 2003, a federal grand jury returned a third superseding indictment which charged Shannahan with ten counts of unlawfully transferring a firearm. Shannahan subsequently plead guilty to all ten counts in the indictment.

Verdict: Guilty on some charges/not guilty on others
Additional details: From Nangarhar Province, Afghanistan; requested compassionate release under 18:3582(c)(1)(A) but the request was denied; two counts dismissed (12:963, 959, 960 and 18:2) and one count found not guilty (21:959(a), 959(a)(2), 960(b)(1)(A) and 18:2);
Short narrative: In 2009, Haji Bagcho, from Nangarhar Province, Afghanistan, was investigated by the DEA for narcotics offenses. The investigation revealed that Bagcho was one of the largest heroin traffickers in the world and manufactured the drug in clandestine laboratories along Afghanistan’s border region with Pakistan. Bagcho sent heroin to more than 20 countries, including the United States. Proceeds from his heroin trafficking were then used to support high-level members of the Taliban to further their insurgency in Afghanistan."Beginning in 2005 and continuing for the next five years, the DEA, in cooperation with Afghan authorities, conducted an investigation of Bagcho’s organization. With the help of cooperating witnesses, the DEA purchased heroin directly from the organization on two occasions, which Bagcho understood was destined for the United States. They also conducted several searches of residences belonging to Bagcho and his associates, recovering evidence consistent with drug trafficking.  During one search, ledgers belonging to the defendant were found. One ledger, cataloguing Bagcho’s activities during 2006, reflected heroin transactions of more than 123,000 kilograms, worth more than $250 million, according to Bagcho’s ledger. Based on heroin production statistics compiled by the United Nations Office of Drugs and Crime for 2006, the defendant’s trafficking accounted for approximately 20% of the world’s total production for that year." (DOJ Press Release). The investigation also obtained evidence that over several years, Bagcho used a portion of his drug proceeds to provide the former Taliban governor of Nangarhar Province and two Taliban commanders responsible for insurgent activity in eastern Afghanistan with cash, weapons and other supplies so that they could continue their “jihad” against western troops and the Afghan government." On January 28, 2010 Haji Bagcho, Sucha Gul, and Zahir Shah were indicted for Conspiracy to Distribute One Kilogram Or More of Heroin Intending and Knowing that the Heroin Will Be Unlawfully Imported into the United States, Knowing and Intending to Provide Anything of Pecuniary Value to a Person or Organization Engaged in Terrorism or Terrorist Activity, Aiding and Abetting, Notice of Forfeiture. All counts charged against Gul and Shah were dismissed without prejudice. In 2012, Bagcho "the Court sentenced the defendant to three terms of life imprisonment, to run concurrently, and sixty months of supervised release as required by statute" (Court Documents, "Government's Response to Defendant's Motion to Reduce Sentence Pursuant to 18 U.S.C 3582(c)(1)(A)(i)"). In December 2015, "the Court entered an Order and Memorandum Opinion granting the defendant's [Bagcho] motion for a new trial as to Count Four of the Superseding Indictment, but denying the defendant's motion as to Count One and Two" after the invalidity of a trial witness's testimony (Court Documents, "Government's Response to Defendant's Motion to Reduce Sentence Pursuant to 18 U.S.C 3582(c)(1)(A)(i)"). The Court recalculated Bagcho's sentence without the reliance of the witness mentioned above, "the Court ultimately rejected the defendant's recommendation of 120 months of incarceration and sentenced the defendant to 300 months of incarceration on each count, to run concurrently" (Court Documents, "Government's Response to Defendant's Motion to Reduce Sentence Pursuant to 18 U.S.C 3582(c)(1)(A)(i)).

Short narrative: On the evening of December 19, 2012, in Oildale, California, white supremacist gang member Justin Cole Whittington, 25, and his step-brother Jesse Lamb--who had both been drinking alcohol outside the scene of the incident earlier in the afternoon--stopped in front of the victim's home in a PT Cruiser. Whittington got out of the car with a sawed-off shotgun, shouted a racial epithet at the victim--who was a Latino man--and fired a round towards the victim while shouting at him to get out of town. Whittington left in the PT Cruiser thereafter. While the victim had not been shot, his wife quickly called the police. Whittington then drove to a nearby convenience store owned by a man of Middle Eastern descent and fired the shotgun again, this time without leaving the vehicle. Whittington was convicted of all four charges in December 2016 and then subsequently sentenced to fifteen years in prison for the crime on April 10, 2017.

Short narrative: Early in the morning on December 26, 2015, Amrik Singh Bal, a 68-year-old Sikh man wearing his full religious garb, was waiting for his ride to work to arrive in Fresno, California. Daniel Coronel Wilson, Jr., 22, and Alexis Mendoza, 17, were driving by in a Dodge Challenger when they spotted Bal, profiling him as an ISIS terrorist as they mistook his Sikh garb for Islamic attire. The Challenger pulled up to Bal, and the two men cursed at and physically attacked Bal; one of them yelled "Why are you here?" as they beat him in the face with their fists. As Bal pleaded for mercy, Wilson and Mendoza returned to the Challenger and rammed Bal with it. As Wilson and Mendoza escaped, Bal laid badly injured and unconscious on the pavement for six minutes before his friends arrived; Bal was hospitalized for a broken collar bone, swollen jaw, and multiple cuts. After three months of investigation, Fresno Police identified Wilson and Mendoza and arrested them. Mendoza, who had been the one driving the vehicle when they rammed Bal with it, was charged with two felony counts of Assault by Means Likely to Produce Great Bodily Injury and Assault with a Deadly Weapon; Mendoza would have been tried as an adult if he had not committed suicide before being able to stand trial.
